name: Dirt Brown
lede: Dirt Brown is named plainly for the color of dry soil, settled on by the crowd-sourced 2010 xkcd color survey rather than any historical dictionary.

sections.title: A plain name for an everyday color
sections.body:
The xkcd online color survey of 2010 asked volunteers to name swatches freehand, and "dirt brown" was one of the straightforward, literal labels that emerged for this moderate yellowish-brown [1]. No older plate, dictionary or traditional system in the books consulted here records this exact hue under this or any related name.

Its closest look-alike on file is [[dresden-brown]], about 2.8 units off, with [[raw-umber]], [[bismarck-brown]] and [[dusty-hazel]] close behind [2]. All sit in the same narrow, muted brown band.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 22.58% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (5,370 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 3,052 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 99% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1300s, present in 23.1% of the 251 paintings we have from that decade (58 paintings), 1.9 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light across its 3,052 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Pedro Berruguete, present in 8 of 20 works here, 2.8x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 2.1x) [3]. The earliest match dates to 799, 1211 years before the name's 2010 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
